events.title: Gore by 2.4
events.text: Al Gore carried Minnesota, 47.9 to 45.5 percent; Ralph Nader won 5.2.

events.title: Wellstone killed
events.text: On 25 October Senator Paul Wellstone and seven others died in a plane crash near Eveleth, eleven days before the election.

events.title: Coleman elected
events.text: Norm Coleman beat Walter Mondale, 49.5 to 47.3 percent: the last Republican to win a U.S. Senate race in Minnesota.

events.title: Kerry by 3.5
events.text: John Kerry carried Minnesota, 51.1 to 47.6 percent.

events.title: School board
events.text: Peggy Flanagan was elected to the Minneapolis school board.

events.title: Pawlenty holds on
events.text: Governor Tim Pawlenty won re-election by 0.96 points: the last statewide win for a Minnesota Republican.

events.title: 312 votes
events.text: Al Franken led Coleman by 312 votes after a recount and an election contest that ran into 2009.

events.title: Franken seated
events.text: On 30 June the Minnesota Supreme Court upheld Franken's win; he was sworn in on 7 July.

events.title: Sunday Night Football
events.text: Michele Tafoya began eleven seasons as NBC's Sunday Night Football sideline reporter.

events.title: Obama's 28 counties
events.text: Barack Obama won Minnesota by 7.7 points and carried 28 counties, including Itasca, Koochiching and Mower.

events.title: Flanagan in the House
events.text: Flanagan won a special election to the Minnesota House from St. Louis Park.

events.title: Clinton by 44,593
events.text: Hillary Clinton carried Minnesota by 1.5 points; Donald Trump carried the Iron Range district.

events.title: Smith appointed
events.text: After Al Franken resigned, Governor Mark Dayton appointed Lieutenant Governor Tina Smith; she was sworn in on 3 January.

events.title: Smith elected
events.text: Smith won the special Senate election, 53.0 to 42.4 percent; Walz and Flanagan were elected governor and lieutenant governor.

events.title: George Floyd
events.text: On 25 May George Floyd was killed by a Minneapolis police officer, who was later convicted of murder.

events.title: Record turnout
events.text: Almost 80 percent of eligible Minnesotans voted, the highest turnout in the country.

events.title: Smith re-elected
events.text: Smith beat Jason Lewis, 48.7 to 43.5 percent; Joe Biden carried the state by 7.1.

events.title: Police vote
events.text: Minneapolis voters rejected replacing the police department, 56 to 44 percent.

events.title: Tafoya leaves NBC
events.text: After Super Bowl LVI, Tafoya retired from broadcasting and co-chaired Kendall Qualls's campaign for governor.

events.title: Walz re-elected
events.text: Walz and Flanagan won a second term by 7.7 points.

events.title: Harris by 4.2
events.text: Kamala Harris carried Minnesota while winning only 9 of its 87 counties.

events.title: Klobuchar by 15.7
events.text: Amy Klobuchar beat Royce White and carried 21 counties; Rebecca Whiting, the Libertarian, won 1.7 percent.

events.title: Smith retires
events.text: On 13 February Senator Tina Smith said she would not run in 2026: 'This decision is not political.'

events.title: Flanagan launches
events.text: On 20 February Lieutenant Governor Flanagan formally launched her Senate campaign.

events.title: Hortman killed
events.text: On 14 June former House Speaker Melissa Hortman and her husband were shot dead in Brooklyn Park, in attacks authorities called politically motivated.

events.title: Fraud charges
events.text: On 18 December federal prosecutors said a large share of $18 billion billed to 14 state-run Medicaid programs might be fraudulent.

events.title: Walz steps aside
events.text: On 5 January Governor Walz ended his bid for a third term.

events.title: Metro Surge
events.text: During a federal immigration operation, federal officers shot dead two U.S. citizens in Minneapolis, Renée Good (7 Jan) and Alex Pretti (24 Jan).

events.title: Tafoya launches
events.text: On 21 January Tafoya, of Edina, entered the Senate race as a Republican.

events.title: Klobuchar runs
events.text: On 29 January Senator Klobuchar announced a run for governor.

events.title: Metro Surge ends
events.text: On 12 February the White House border czar announced the end of the operation.

events.title: Bock sentenced
events.text: On 21 May Aimee Bock, founder of Feeding Our Future, was sentenced to more than 41 years for a child-nutrition fraud.

events.title: Two conventions
events.text: On 29 May Republicans in Duluth endorsed Adam Schwarze over Tafoya; on 30 May the DFL endorsed Flanagan in Rochester.

events.title: Convention in Duluth
events.text: The Republican convention endorsed Schwarze on the sixth ballot; Tafoya ran in the primary anyway.

events.title: Primary day
events.text: On 11 August Flanagan beat Rep. Angie Craig, 59 to 39 percent; Tafoya won 52 percent in a nine-way Republican race.

events.title: Voting begins
events.text: Absentee and early voting began on 18 September; by 16 October, 202,252 ballots had been accepted.

events.title: Lean Democratic
events.text: Inside Elections (1 Oct), Sabato's Crystal Ball (14 Oct) and the Cook Political Report (20 Oct) moved the race to Lean Democratic.

events.title: Trump endorses Tafoya
events.text: On 12 October President Trump urged Minnesotans to vote for Tafoya at a rally in Youngstown, Ohio.

events.title: The only debate
events.text: On 16 October Flanagan and Tafoya met in their only debate before Election Day, at MPR News in St. Paul.

events.title: Election Day
events.text: On 3 November Minnesotans choose between Flanagan, Tafoya, Whiting and Simonetti.

eras: Upheaval, record turnout, a narrowing map
An open seat: Flanagan vs Tafoya
chartNote: Each state is coloured by the margin of the most recent presidential popular vote (Democratic minus Republican share of all votes; FEC certified results). It is a simplification: Minnesota elects its senator in its own race, and many Minnesotans split their tickets (in 2024 the DFL Senate margin was about eleven points larger than the DFL presidential margin), so the presidential colour is a backdrop, not a forecast. Shares are of land area, not of people or votes. Boundaries are today's states (Natural Earth); the map is framed on Minnesota, so outer states are cut at the edge.
